title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
book: NCERT First Flight: Textbook in English for Class X
subject: english_literature
author: Anne Frank
syllabus_note: CBSE 2025-26 English Language and Literature (184): First Flight prose, Chapter 4. Assessed through extracts (5 marks), short answers in 40-50 words (3 marks) and long answers in 100-120 words (6 marks).

blocks.title: 'Paper has more patience than people'
blocks.body:
On her **thirteenth birthday** a girl in Amsterdam received a diary. She named it **Kitty** and wrote to it as her closest friend.

Two years later she was dead, a victim of the Nazi persecution of Jews. Her diary survived and is now read in more than 70 languages. In this chapter we read the opening pages: why she writes, her family, and a funny battle with a maths teacher.

blocks.title: The writer
blocks.body:
**Anne Frank** was born in Frankfurt, Germany, on **12 June 1929**. Her Jewish family moved to Amsterdam in Holland in 1933 to escape the Nazis. From 1942 they hid in a secret annexe; in 1944 they were discovered. Anne died in the **Bergen-Belsen** concentration camp in 1945.

Her father **Otto Frank**, the only survivor of the family, published her diary, written in **Dutch**. It is one of the most widely read books in the world.
blocks.future: Writing a journal builds clear thinking and honest expression, skills used by writers, journalists and historians.

blocks.question: Anne had loving parents, a sister and about thirty friends, yet she felt alone. How is that possible?
options: She could not share her deepest feelings with any of them
She did not like her friends at all
blocks.explanation: She lacked one true friend to confide in, so she turned to her diary.

blocks.title: Saturday, 20 June 1942
blocks.body:
**A strange experience:** Anne says writing a diary is strange for someone like her: she has never written anything before, and she thinks neither she nor anyone else will be interested in 'the musings of a thirteen-year-old schoolgirl'.

**'Paper has more patience than people.'** She remembers this saying from a day when she sat at home, bored and low, unsure whether to stay in or go out. Paper will listen without getting tired.

**No real friend:** she has loving parents, a sixteen-year-old sister and about thirty people she can call friends, and admirers too, but she cannot get close to anyone. With friends she talks only of ordinary things. 'That's the root of the problem.' So the diary will be her friend, and she names it **Kitty**.

**Not a list of facts:** she does not want to jot down facts in a diary 'the way most people would do'; she wants the diary itself to be her friend. So she first gives Kitty a **brief sketch of her life**.

blocks.question: Why did Anne name her diary 'Kitty'?
options: it was the name of the shop
she wanted the diary to be her close friend
blocks.explanation: She wanted to confide in it as in a friend.

blocks.question: What does 'paper has more patience than people' mean?
options: you can write anything on paper and it will not get tired of listening
blocks.explanation: Anne remembered this saying on a day she felt bored and low.
option_feedback: It is about listening, not time.

blocks.title: Family sketch and the chatterbox essays
blocks.body:
**Family:** her father married at 36, her mother at 25. Her sister **Margot** was born in **Frankfurt** in 1926; Anne on **12 June 1929**. Being **Jewish**, the family emigrated to **Holland in 1933**, where her father became Managing Director of the **Dutch Opekta Company**, which made products used in making jam. Her **grandmother** came to live with them and died in **January 1942**; no one knows how often Anne thinks of her. Her birthday in 1942 was celebrated to make up for the one in 1941, and a candle was lit for her grandmother.

**School:** she went to a **Montessori nursery school** and stayed there until the sixth form, when her teacher was the headmistress **Mrs Kuperus**; they had a tearful farewell. Later she went to the **Jewish Lyceum**.

**Mr Keesing:** her old maths teacher was annoyed because she talked so much. As punishment he gave her an essay, **'A Chatterbox'**. Anne argued that talking is a student's trait and that she had inherited it from her mother, so she could never be cured. Mr Keesing laughed, but when she went on talking he assigned **'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'**, and then **'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterback'**. With her friend **Sanne**, good at poetry, she wrote a poem about a mother duck and a father swan with three baby ducklings who were bitten to death by their father because they quacked too much. Mr Keesing took the joke the right way, read the poem aloud to the class, and from then on **allowed her to talk** and gave her no more extra homework.

blocks.title: The people in Anne's sketch
blocks.body:
| Person | What Anne tells Kitty |
|---|---|
| **Father (Otto Frank)** | 'the most adorable father I've ever seen'; married at 36; became Managing Director of the Dutch Opekta Company |
| **Mother (Edith)** | married at 25; Anne says she inherited her talkativeness from her mother |
| **Margot** | her elder sister, born in 1926 in Frankfurt; brilliant report card |
| **Grandmother** | came to live with them; died in January 1942; Anne lit a candle for her on her birthday |
| **Mrs Kuperus** | headmistress of her Montessori school; their parting was tearful |
| **Mr Keesing** | old-fogey maths teacher; set essays on 'chatterbox' as punishment, then laughed at her poem |

blocks.title: Three punishments, three clever replies
blocks.body:
| Punishment | Anne's answer |
|---|---|
| **'A Chatterbox'** | talking is a student's trait; she will try, but may never be cured, as her mother talks as much |
| **'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'** | she wrote it and handed it in; Mr Keesing had no complaints for two lessons |
| **'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterback'** | a poem (with her friend Sanne) about a mother duck and a father swan, who bit his three quacking ducklings to death; Mr Keesing took the joke well |

blocks.question: Why was Mr Keesing annoyed with Anne?
options: she talked too much in class
blocks.explanation: So he gave her essays on being a chatterbox.
option_feedback: He was annoyed by her talking.

blocks.question: How did Anne justify talking in her first essay?
options: talking is a student's trait, and she had inherited it from her mother
blocks.explanation: Her argument was clever and amusing.

blocks.title: What the diary shows about Anne
blocks.body:
- **Thoughtful and honest:** she looks into her own feelings ('We don't seem to be able to get any closer, and that's the problem').
- **Lonely:** many friends but no confidant.
- **Loving:** she adores her father and misses her grandmother.
- **Witty and confident:** she turns punishment into clever essays and a poem.
- **Mature beyond her age:** she sees through people and writes with insight.

| Word or phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **musings** | thoughts, reflections |
| **confide** | to share secrets with someone you trust |
| **listless** | without energy |
| **brooding** | thinking deeply, often sadly |
| **incorrigible** | that cannot be corrected or changed |
| **old fogey** | an old-fashioned person |
| **chatterbox** | someone who talks too much |
| **ingenious** | very clever |

blocks.question: 'Incorrigible' means:
blocks.explanation: 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox' was the second essay.
option_feedback: It means the opposite of improving.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Dates: born 12 June 1929; diary entry 20 June 1942; moved to Holland 1933; grandmother died January 1942.**
- **Essays: Chatterbox → Incorrigible Chatterbox → Quack, Quack, Quack (poem with Sanne).**
- **Teachers: Mrs Kuperus (kind, tearful farewell); Mr Keesing (maths, punishments, then a good sport).**
- **Diary = Kitty; language = Dutch.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Writing that Anne had no friends: she had about **thirty friends**, but no one to confide in.
2. Calling Mr Keesing cruel: he was annoyed, but he **took the poem as a joke** and let her talk.
3. Saying the diary was written in English: it was written in **Dutch**.
4. Mixing up Margot (sister) and Kitty (the diary).

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Ask each student to write a four-line diary entry about one school day, addressed to a named diary. Then discuss: how is writing to 'a friend' different from listing facts?

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Is a diary a good substitute for a friend? What can a diary give you that a friend cannot, and what can a friend give that a diary cannot?

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **History (The Rise of Nationalism in Europe):** extreme nationalism later led to the Nazi persecution that Anne's family fled.
- **Nelson Mandela (Ch 2):** another life story of resisting injustice.
- **Writing:** diary entries are a common creative task.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
'Anne was right that no one would be interested in the musings of a thirteen-year-old schoolgirl.' Do you agree? Answer in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** No, Anne was wrong, though she could not have known it. She thought a schoolgirl's thoughts would interest no one, so she wrote mainly for herself and for 'Kitty'. But her honest, lively diary became one of the most widely read books in the world. Readers value it because it shows the everyday feelings of a teenager, such as loneliness, love for her father and fun with a strict teacher, against the dark background of the Nazi persecution of Jews. Her wit, as in the 'Quack, Quack, Quack' poem, and her insight into people make her real to us. Her diary turned a private voice into a lasting record of history.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Anne Frank, given a diary on her 13th birthday, names it Kitty and makes it her friend because she cannot confide in anyone.
- 'Paper has more patience than people.'
- She sketches her family: German Jews who moved to Holland in 1933; her father, mother, sister Margot and beloved grandmother.
- At school, Mr Keesing punishes her talkativeness with three essays; her clever poem wins him over and he lets her talk.
- The diary shows Anne as honest, lonely, loving, witty and mature.

blocks.title: Exam tips
blocks.body:
- For questions on Anne's character, pair each quality with an example (witty: the duck poem; loving: candle for grandmother).
- Remember the order and titles of the three essays; questions often ask about them.
- For 'Is Mr Keesing unpredictable?', show his change: punishment → laughter → acceptance.

blocks.front: Why did Anne feel lonely though she had many friends?
blocks.back: She could not confide her deepest feelings in any of them; they talked only of ordinary things.

blocks.front: What were the three essays Mr Keesing set?
blocks.back: 'A Chatterbox', 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox' and 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterback'.

blocks.front: In what language was the diary written?
How did Mr Keesing react to the duck poem?
blocks.back: He took it as a joke, read it to the class and allowed Anne to talk from then on.
